questions.q: What does process creation telemetry capture beyond the fact that a process started?
options: Full command-line arguments, parent process, user context, and a precise timestamp
Only the file size of the executable that ran
Nothing else — EDR logs process starts the same way antivirus logs a scan
A list of every file the process might open in the future
questions.explain: EDR records the exact command line a process launched with, its parent process, the user context, and the timestamp — not just the executable's name.

questions.q: Why is "powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -EncodedCommand ..." more concerning than "powershell.exe" alone?
options: Only full command-line visibility reveals the hidden window and encoded payload, not just that PowerShell ran
PowerShell with no arguments is always malicious
The two commands run on different operating systems
EDR cannot see command-line arguments at all
questions.explain: Capturing the full command line, not just the process name, is what lets an analyst tell a routine PowerShell launch apart from an obfuscated, hidden one.

questions.q: What does network connection telemetry pair together to make it useful?
options: The destination, port, and protocol of a connection together with the exact process that opened it
Only the total number of bytes sent across the whole network
The physical location of the server, with no process information
A list of every website ever visited by any user on the network
questions.explain: Tying a connection's destination and port to the specific process that opened it is what lets an unusual pairing — like certutil.exe reaching an unfamiliar address — stand out.

questions.q: Why does registry telemetry matter for catching persistence mechanisms?
options: Malware often adds itself to a Run key or scheduled task to survive a reboot, and watching those writes catches it as it happens
The registry has no connection to how malware survives a reboot
Registry telemetry only tracks user login times
Persistence mechanisms never touch the registry
questions.explain: Watching writes to persistence-related registry keys lets EDR catch the moment malware sets itself up to run again, long before the next reboot.

questions.q: What does DLL/module load telemetry catch that file-based scanning misses entirely?
options: Process injection and DLL side-loading, where malicious code loads into a trusted process's memory without ever existing as a new file on disk
Files that are too large for antivirus to scan
Network connections made over encrypted channels
Registry keys that were deleted rather than created
questions.explain: When malicious code is loaded directly into an already-trusted running process, there's no new file for a scanner to examine — only module-load telemetry reveals it happened.
